• The apostle exhorts believers to encourage and bear up their fainting spirits on the Lord and the power of His might.
• He explains how to do this by putting on the whole armor of God.

••II. The Importance of Being Armed••

• A Christian must be armed for the war against sin and Satan.
• Without Christ, a person is naked and unarmed, unfit to fight Christ's battles.

••III. The Furniture of Armor••

• The furniture or armor needed is Christ.
• Christ is the Lord Jesus, who is to be put on as armor (Rom. 13:14).

••IV. The Kind or Quality of Armor••

• The graces of Christ are the armor, including:
	• The girdle of truth
	• The breastplate of righteousness
	• The rest of the armor

••V. The Quantity or Entireness of Armor••

• The whole armor of God is needed to stand against the wiles of the devil.
• A Christian must put on the whole armor, not just a part of it.

••VI. The Use of Armor••

• The armor must be put on, not just thought about or wished for.
• A Christian must conscientiously use the means appointed for their defense.

••VII. The Consequences of Not Being Armed••

• A person without Christ is naked and unarmed, unable to make head against sin and Satan.
• They are at the will of Satan, a subdued people disarmed by their proud conqueror.

••VIII. The Example of the Fanatic Spirit••

• The fanatic spirit at Munster was a poor example of a Christian, rushing into battle without armor.
• They trusted in God, but were not armed with the whole armor of God.

••IX. The Importance of Humility••

• A Christian must not trust in their own strength or confidence, but in the power of God.
• They must be humble and acknowledge their need for the armor of God.

••X. The Result of Being Armed••

• A Christian who puts on the whole armor of God will be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
• They will be strong in the Lord and able to make head against sin and Satan.

• The principle of holiness is a supernatural principle
• It is distinct from Adam's righteousness and holiness, which was natural to him
• Holiness is a natural result of being a child of God

••2. The Source of Holiness••

• The Spirit of God plants this principle of holiness in the heart of a child of God
• The Spirit is sent by God to indwell believers, making them children of God
• This indwelling Spirit is the source of true holiness

••3. The Efficacy of Holiness••

• The principle of holiness is ever endeavouring to act in the heart of a child of God
• It is not a dull habit, but a living and active principle that bears fruit
• The Spirit's work in the heart is not a one-time event, but an ongoing process

••4. The Imperfect Nature of Holiness••

• The principle of holiness is imperfect, enabling only an endeavour, not a full performance
• It makes the creature willing, but not always able, to give full obedience
• The saints' hearts leap to do God's will, but often creep in the way of God's commandments

••5. The Uniformity of Holiness••

• True holiness does not divide what God has joined together
• A sanctified heart desires to be a faithful executor of God's will
• It seeks to perform the whole will of God, not just part of it

••6. The Order of Holiness••

• The principle of holiness first acts towards God, and then towards man
• It seeks to serve God in righteousness and charity, and then to serve man
• The order of holiness is to first give oneself to the Lord, and then to serve others by the will of God

• Evangelical holiness makes the creature rather willing than able to give full obedience
• The saints' hearts are willing to do what is holy and righteous, but often struggle to do so
• The principle of holiness is not a guarantee of perfection, but a willingness to strive for it

••8. The Fruit of Holiness••

• The principle of holiness bears fruit in the life of a child of God
• It produces a willingness to serve God and others, and to do what is holy and righteous
• The fruit of holiness is not a one-time event, but an ongoing process

••9. The Claim of Holiness••

• The saints can claim a good conscience, willing to live honestly and righteously
• They trust that they have a good conscience, even if they do not fully attain to it
• The claim of holiness is not a guarantee of perfection, but a willingness to strive for it

••10. The Interpretation of Holiness••

• The law allows for no good conscience, but the gospel interprets the law in a favourable light
• The principle of holiness seeks to serve God in righteousness and charity, and then to serve others by the will of God
• The interpretation of holiness is not a one-time event, but an ongoing process.

••1. The Nature of Unbelief••

• Unbelief is a sin that remains even after outward acts of sin have disappeared.
• The guilt of unbelief remains until faith strikes it off with the blood of Christ.

••2. The Power of Unbelief••

• The power of lusts remains as long as one is an unbeliever, even if outward acts of sin disappear.
• The heart is not emptied of sin, but the vent is stopped by restraining grace.

••3. The Futility of Mortifying Lusts••

• It is impossible to truly mortify any lust without faith, which is the only victory over the world.
• Unbelievers may think they have overcome sin, but in reality, the sin remains.

••4. The Liar••

• Unbelievers bear false witness against God himself by denying the truth of the gospel.
• This is a more grievous lie than any other, as it involves denying the truth of God's promises.

••5. The Murderer••

• Unbelievers are more bloody murderers than those who have committed physical murder.
• They kill Christ over again by their unbelief and tread his blood under their feet.

••6. The Nature of Unregenerate Man••

• The unregenerate person may try to wipe off guilt by saying it's not their fault they don't keep commands.
• However, this is a false inference, as they are still responsible for their sin.

••7. The Cause of Inability••

• Man's inability to obey is not created by God, but contracted by the creature himself.
• Man was made upright, but he has sought out many inventions to justify his sin.

••8. God's Right to Command••

• God has not lost his power to command, even if man has lost his ability to obey.
• Man's fault cannot prejudice God's right to command.

••9. The Excuse of Inability••

• Man's present impotency to yield obedience to God's commands does not afford him an excuse.
• This inability is not a disability created by God, but a result of man's own unmeetness.

••10. The Consequences of Unbelief••

• Unbelief is a sin that will be punished, and God will be paid his debt, either by the unbeliever or by Christ for the unbeliever.
• Christ pays no reckoning for unbelievers, and they will be held accountable for their unbelief.

••1. The Holiness of God••

• The holiness of God is a attribute that faith must answer.
• Faith must answer two things about God's holiness:
	• That God's holiness makes him hate sin, yet incline his heart to show mercy to sinners.
	• That God's holiness is no enemy to pardoning mercy.

••2. God's Holiness and Mercy••

• God's holiness does not make him hard-hearted to sinners.
• God's holiness obliges him to be faithful in all his promises.
• The holiness of God is the strongest argument for the truth and faithfulness of his promises.

••3. God's Promises••

• God's promises are founded in his holiness and are therefore sure mercies.
• The reason for man's unfaithfulness in promises is some unholiness in his heart.
• A good God will be as good as his word.

••4. God's Covenant with Jacob••

• God's covenant with Jacob was inviolably kept, despite Jacob's unfaithfulness.
• This was because God had to deal with a holy God, not a sinful man.

••5. The Attribute of Justice••

• The attribute of justice seems little to befriend the pardoning act of God's mercy.
• The naked consideration of God's justice without a gospel comment can appall and dispirit the awakened sinner.

••6. The Fear of God's Justice••

• The fear of God's justice can be a matter of amazement to the awakened sinner.
• The thought of God's justice without a gospel comment can fill the heart with horror.

••7. The Gospel Comment••

• The gospel comment is necessary to safely and comfortably view God's justice.
• The gospel comment shows that God's justice is not an enemy to pardoning mercy.

••8. God's Justice and Mercy••

• God's justice and mercy are not mutually exclusive.
• God's justice is the foundation of his mercy.

••9. The Holiness of God and Forgiveness••

• The holiness of God makes forgiveness difficult, but not impossible.
• The holiness of God is the reason why God's mercy is sure and faithful.

••10. The Comfort of God's Promises••

• The promises of God are a comfort to the poor and trembling soul.
• The holiness of God is the strongest argument for the truth and faithfulness of God's promises.

••I. Asserting the Truth of the Point••

	• This means that there is only one mediator (Christ) and one Spirit (the Holy Ghost) that can pray for us.
• Jesus rebuked the disciples for their rash motion, saying they did not know what manner of spirit they were of (Luke 9:55).
	• This implies that prayer must be guided by the Holy Spirit.

••II. The Importance of the Spirit in Prayer••

• The name of Christ is not more necessary than the Spirit of Christ in prayer.
	• Christ's name is only spoken by the Spirit's mouth, and it is too great a word for anyone to speak without the Spirit's help.
• To say "Jesus is Lord" requires the Spirit of God to be in one's heart and tongue.
	• This means that mere repetition of Christ's name without faith and the Spirit's guidance is not sufficient.

••III. The Role of the Spirit in Prayer••

• The Spirit is the key that unlocks the door to God's presence.
	• Faith is the key that turns the key, but the Spirit is the one who makes this key and helps the Christian to turn it in prayer.
• The Spirit is the one who helps the Christian to offer up prayers and praises to God.
	• This is compared to the incense and fire in Leviticus 10:1, which signified the merit and satisfaction of Christ.

••IV. The Two Ways the Spirit Helps in Prayer••

• The Spirit helps in prayer by his gifts.
	• These gifts are either extraordinary or ordinary.
• The extraordinary gifts of the Spirit in prayer were shed forth in the primitive times.
	• These gifts included the ability to pray and preach in a miraculous manner.
• The ordinary gift of the Spirit in prayer is a special faculty that enables persons to form their thoughts and desires into apt words before the Lord in prayer.
	• This gift is common and is bestowed on those who are not necessarily the best men.
